subject: computer-science

moments.title: Smalltalk at PARC
moments.who: Alan Kay, Dan Ingalls, Adele Goldberg, Xerox PARC
moments.body: Kay's team at Xerox PARC develops Smalltalk, the first fully object-oriented language. Everything is an object; everything communicates by sending messages. The Alto workstation that ran Smalltalk also pioneered the bitmap display, mouse, GUI, WYSIWYG editing and Ethernet — all in 1973.
moments.takeaway: Almost every interface element on every screen you've ever used was prototyped at Xerox PARC by 1975. Xerox failed to commercialise any of it.

moments.title: Steve Jobs visits PARC
moments.body: Jobs and a small Apple team are shown the Xerox Alto in a famous December 1979 visit. They focus on the GUI; they miss object-oriented programming, the network and SmallTalk's deep ideas. The Lisa (1983) and Macintosh (1984) borrow the GUI; Microsoft borrows from the Mac.

quote.text: Good artists copy, great artists steal.
quote.attrib: Steve Jobs, attributed (he attributed it to Picasso)

moments.takeaway: The most influential computer demo in history transferred ideas from a research lab that could not productise them to a startup that could.

now.title: OOP today
now.body: Object-oriented programming dominated language design from C++ (1979) and Java (1995) through the 2000s. Functional programming has reasserted itself (Scala, Kotlin, Rust traits, JavaScript). 'Composition over inheritance' is now mainstream advice. Kay has long argued real OOP — messages between objects — has not been widely understood.
now.open_questions: Does the next interface paradigm exist somewhere already, prototyped and unrecognised?

reflection: Alan Kay's 1972 vision of the 'Dynabook' — a personal, networked, tablet-sized computer for children — directly anticipated the iPad (2010, by 38 years). Kay was at Apple at the time but the iPad team did not consult him.
